etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Reduplication of 刺 (ira, “thorn”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from 怪事 (keji, “unfortunate event”). Used in the Edo period to mean "a shabby, lowborn individual" before taking on the current sense.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Most likely of onomatopoeic origin; compare すきすき (sukisuki, “refreshingly”) and すきっと (sukitto, “refreshingly”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Wasei eigo (和製英語; pseudo-anglicism), derived from gasoline + stand. Attested from at least 1933.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English campus. Doublet of キャンプ (kyanpu, “camp”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English ball pen.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *poka.
Related to Baekje ホカ (*poka, “outside”), compare Korean 밖 (bak, “outside”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 他 (MC tha).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Analyzable as the irregular -ba conditional conjugation of verb 例える (tatoeru, “to compare something, to liken one thing to another, to make a metaphor about something”).
Historically, the term appears from at least the late Heian period in the Kokin Wakashū dated roughly 920 CE, indicating that the original derivation was as the regular -ba conditional conjugation of Old Japanese-derived verb 例ふ (tatofu), conjugated in the 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern. Through regular historical processes, classical 例ふ (tatofu) evolved into modern 例える (tatoeru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 内(ない) (nai, “internal”) + 線(せん) (sen, “line”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 凍る (koporu).
Likely cognate with other terms beginning with ko- and related to senses of hard, stiff, such as 凝(こ)る (koru, “to stiffen”), 凍(こ)ゆ (koyu, “to freeze, to become frozen”, classical) → modern 凍(こご)える (kogoeru), 強(こわ)い (kowai, “hard, tough, stiff”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Chinese 國會 /国会 (guóhuì).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Korean 국회 (Gukhoe).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Vietnamese Quốc hội.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Shift from verb 存ず (zonzu).
Natural progression from サ行変格活用 (sa-gyō henkaku katsuyō, “s-irregular conjugation”) verbs ending in -uru to 上一段活用 (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 尋ぬ (tazunu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 彼(かれ) (kare) + 等(ら) (-ra)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shortened from 教科用(きょうかよう)図書(としょ) (kyōka-yō tosho).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 明(あ)かる (akaru, “to become bright”).
This term originally referred to natural light, while the sense of lamp or lighting was expressed using the term 灯火 (tomoshibi, literally “set alight + fire”). The term akari gained its modern lighting sense during the late Edo period, and has now largely displaced tomoshibi for this sense.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/putuː/ → /fut͡suː/
From Middle Chinese compound 普通 (MC phuX thuwng, literally “ordinary + through”). Compare modern Hakka phû-thûng, Cantonese pou² tung¹, Mandarin pǔtōng.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 来 (rai-, “coming..., next...”) + 週 (shū, “week”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 註 (MC tsyuH|trjuH). 注 is a daiyōji replacing 註.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kwasai/ → /kasai/
From Middle Chinese compound 火災 (xwa^X tsoj). Compare modern Mandarin reading huǒzāi.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese compound 真劍 (MC tsyin kjaemH, “real sword”). Compare modern Mandarin 真劍／真剑 (zhēnjiàn).
The original meaning was real sword. Over time, this shifted, and the term is now often used to mean serious.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Shift from watakushi below.
This reading was already prevalent in early modern times, possibly around the mid-late Muromachi to early-Edo period.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 私 (watakusi).
A surface analysis suggests a compound term. However, no likely etyma are known.
* From first-person pronoun 我 (wa, “I, me”) + takusi: although the first element seems likely, the original meaning of watakushi was “private”, as opposed to “public”, with no first-person pronoun usage until the late 13th century.
* From 我(わ) (wa, “I, me”) + つ (tsu, “genitive marker”), and the other parts remain unknown.
* From wata + kusi: the only phonetic matches are 綿 (wata, “cotton; cotton batting”), 腸 (wata, “guts, one's innards”, likely derived from the “batting” sense), 海 (wata, “sea, ocean”) + 串 (kusi, “skewer”), 奇し (kusi, “magic, fantastic, supernatural”, adjective), 酒 (kusi, “alcoholic beverage”, likely derived from the “magic” sense), 櫛 (kusi, “comb”).
* The first element may come from 内(うち) (uchi, “one's own, my, our”), and the second element remains unknown.
The meaning evolved over time from “private” or “privatization”, to refer to things that are personal, to refer to one's own person, and then finally to serve as a generic first-person pronoun. The full form watakushi is still used in modern Japanese as a formal, highly polite first-person pronoun. The abbreviated form watashi is now the most common and neutrally polite first-person pronoun.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/si/ → /ɕi/
From Middle Chinese 私 (MC sij).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
窓(まど) (mado, “window”) + 口(くち) (kuchi, “mouth, opening”).
The kuchi changes to guchi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/tubasa/ → /t͡subasa/
From Old Japanese.
Possibly a shift from a compound of 鳥(と) (to, “bird”) + 総(ふさ) (fusa, “tassel”), though the vowel change is irregular.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 翼 (MC yik).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Nominalization of classical verb 助く (tasuku), modern 助ける (tasukeru, “to assist, help; rescue, save”).

etymologies.text:
In late Middle Japanese, the initial [zo] temporarily becomes affricate [dʒo].
/zauri/ → /zoːri/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with Japanese 侘びる (wabiru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Originally referred to "flat" in reference to flat land, in turn the core meaning of the kanji character.
The alternative 碌 spelling is an example of ateji.
First attested in the 羅葡日辞書 (Ra-Ho-Nichi Jisho, “Latin-Portuguese-Japanese Dictionary”) of 1595.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Substitute spelling for 六 (roku, “six”), likely borrowed from similar usage of written Chinese 陸 /陆 (“six”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 陸 (MC ljuwk). First attested in Japanese as a standalone noun in a text from the mid-1400s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*⟨kuniga⟩ → *⟨kunuga⟩ → /kunuɡa/ → */kunɡa/ → /kuɡa/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
Shift from Old Japanese 陸 (kunuga), also attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, itself a shift from *kuniga, a compound of 国 (kuni, “country, land”) + 処 (-ka, suffix indicating place). The ka changes to ga as an instance of rendaku (連濁). The shift to kunuga may have been by analogy to 国内(くぬち) (kunuchi), whose pronunciation is explainable by regular Old Japanese vowel elision processes.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Classical Japanese verb 離(はな)る (hanaru).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 需要 (MC sju 'jiewH).
